content:
Hi everyone! Our AI4Math team at BICMR@PKU, led by Prof. Bin Dong, is excited to introduce an automated framework that integrates informal reasoning with formal verification. Using this framework, we automatically resolve an open conjecture in commutative algebra posed by D.D. Anderson in 2014. The resulting proof is fully formalized and verified in Lean 4 with essentially no human intervention.

The framework consists of two agents. The formal agent, Archon, was previously released and validated its formalization ability on the FirstProof benchmark (Problems 4 and 6). The informal reasoning agent, Rethlas, mimics the workflow of human mathematicians and is responsible for exploring proof strategies and producing candidate proofs. Both agents are built around key components designed for mathematical research: retrieval tools (Matlas, a semantic search engine over millions of mathematical statements, and LeanSearch, a widely adopted theorem retrieval tool in the Lean community), customizable reasoning skills, and context management mechanisms for sustained long-horizon reasoning.

Anderson’s Problem 8a is proposed in  Open Problems in Commutative Ring Theory (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4939-0925-4_20) in 2014 and has been open since then. Our framework provides a negative answer by constructing a counterexample: using Jensen’s (2006) characterization of formal fibers of completions of UFDs, we construct a local UFD A with completion T = ℂ[[x,y,z]]/(x²−yz) that is weakly quasi-complete but not quasi-complete. The formalization comprises approximately 19,000 lines of Lean 4 code, with a total cost of $600,  covering key results from six external papers, verified by the official Lean Comparator.

Some notable findings: Rethlas, via Matlas, discovered a non-trivial connection between between the theory of quasi-completeness and Jensen’s method of constructing pathological UFDs via completion. Meanwhile, during formalization, Archon used LeanSearch to confirm that Krull domain theory was absent from Mathlib, and then independently identified the Kaplansky criterion as an alternative proof route — a strategy not found in any of the reference papers. See the full report for details.

arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03789
Blog: https://frenzymath.com/blog/conjecture/
Rethlas source: https://github.com/frenzymath/Rethlas
Archon source: https://github.com/frenzymath/Archon
Formlization Results: https://github.com/frenzymath/Anderson-Conjecture

Interesting result (and datapoint for AI formalization)! Would you think that in a world, where all (research) math was formalized, the Informal + Formal Agent Workflow would still be better? Or would a tighter feedback loop with only a Formal Agent be more effective?

You report here that the cost of the formalization was 600$, but in your blogpost you report to have only used 70% of a 1 Week Quota for 3 Claude Max Subscription so wouldn't a 600⋅70400=105600 \cdot \frac{70}{400}=105600⋅40070​=105 $ Cost be more representative? Or upper bounding it a bit a cost of 150$?

Or upper bounding it a bit a cost of 150$?

If all mathematics were fully formalized, it is plausible that a purely formal agent could already generate new results through a tight feedback loop within the formal system.

For the cost of formalization, we subscribed to three Claude Max plans for the project, so that’s $600 in total. But as you pointed out, the actual usage comes out to roughly $105, so the $600 is more like the budget we allocated rather than the effective cost.

Thank you for setting up things so that comparator is very easy to run on this repo! Did anyone independently do this?

Update: I used this as an excuse to learn about comparator and have now done this myself :-)

Your solution is okay!

I very much agree. The philosophy of just presenting the statement and letting the proof be abstracted away by trusting comparator / lean, is very much aligned with my views, on what the powers of Lean can hold in an AI Slop filled world.

And this repo shows an example of how easy it is to technically achieve this and showcase it.

Exciting work! I have a question about the precise meaning of “automatic.” My understanding is that the final Lean proof is machine-checked, but the correctness still depends on whether the formal definitions and theorem statement faithfully capture the intended informal mathematics. Do you manually check only the short top-level specification, such as Challenge.lean, or do you also audit important AI-generated auxiliary definitions?

Also, could you clarify what kinds of guidance were available to the agents during the Anderson experiment? For example, did the agents receive only general tools/prompts/retrieval mechanisms, or were any problem-specific mathematical hints or proof directions provided during the run? This distinction seems important for interpreting the claim of “automatic” or “essentially no human involvement.”

Thank you for the question. We manually checked all definitions in the formalization, including auxiliary ones, to ensure the formal statement matches the intended mathematics.

For the Anderson experiment, the informal agent was given no problem-specific mathematical hints or proof directions. Its only input was the problem statement.

For the formalization agent, the only human intervention during the run was logistical: the agent attempted to download some PDF files needed as references but could not access them directly, so a human downloaded the PDFs and placed them in the project directory.
